analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $35 a month, bans insulin deductibles and prior authorization, and speeds cheaper insulin copies to market.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 28 cosponsors — 14 Republicans, 13 Democrats, 1 Independent — cleared the Senate health committee and now sits on the Senate calendar waiting for a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every private health plan to cover at least one insulin in each dosage form for no more than $35 per 30-day supply, with no deductible and no prior-authorization hoops, and would count insulin payments toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums. It would also make it harder for brand-name drug companies to file petitions that delay approval of competing biosimilar insulins, speed up review of those biosimilars, and fund a ten-state pilot program, a national hotline, and a GAO study to get affordable insulin to uninsured people. The committee's rewrite delayed the $35 cap from 2027 to 2028 and dropped the original's rule that middlemen hand 100% of insulin rebates back to health plans.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million Americans who use insulin through employer, individual, or Marketplace plans would pay at most $35 a month for the insulin types their plan selects, get it without meeting a deductible or fighting a prior authorization, and have those payments count toward their deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Uninsured people in ten states would get help through a $100 million grant program, a 24/7 hotline, and a resource center, and all patients would benefit over time from faster competition from biosimilar insulins.

how_it_helps.text: Group, individual, and Marketplace catastrophic plans must cover selected insulin products with no deductible and cost-sharing capped at $35 per 30-day supply (or, after 2028, the lesser of $35 or 25% of the negotiated net price).
Plans and issuers may not impose prior authorization or medical-management requirements on selected insulin products except for clinically justified safety reasons and reasonable quantity limits.

Cost-sharing paid for selected insulin must count toward the plan's deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, and catastrophic plans must cover selected insulin before a person meets the annual deductible.

The bill rewrites FDA 'citizen petition' rules so that petitions used primarily to delay approval of generic or biosimilar competitors are identified as delaying tactics, with a 180-day filing deadline and required dismissal of lawsuits that skip the petition process.

The FDA may expedite development and review of biosimilars designated as 'competitive biosimilar therapies' for products with fewer than three biosimilar competitors, including faster facility reinspections.

A five-year, $100 million pilot program would give grants to 10 states with high uninsured and diabetes rates to dispense insulin at $35 or less per month through community health centers and retail pharmacies.
The bill funds a 24/7 national hotline and resource center to connect uninsured people with insulin assistance programs, funded at $2 million per year.
The Comptroller General must study and report to Congress on the characteristics, locations, and incomes of uninsured people who use insulin.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer plans bear the cost of covering selected insulin at the $35 cap with no deductible, which would likely show up partly in premiums since the bill contains no federal funding to offset it. Brand-name insulin makers lose monopoly protections as FDA review of biosimilars is expedited and delay tactics are curtailed. Pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators would have lost rebate revenue under the original bill's full pass-through requirement, though the committee rewrite dropped that section.

drawbacks.text: Plans choose which insulin products are 'selected' — one per dosage form and type — so they can steer patients to whichever product the manufacturer gives the best rebate on, while charging full cost-sharing on every other insulin.
The bill excludes out-of-network insulin purchases from the protections, so patients filling outside their plan's network get no cap.
The committee rewrite pushed the $35 cap from plan years beginning 2027 to plan years beginning 2028, delaying relief for patients by a year.

The committee rewrite deleted the original Title II requirement that PBMs and insurers remit 100% of insulin rebates, fees, and discounts back to the health plan with disclosure and audit rights — the provision that would have surfaced and returned the middleman take.
The pilot program for uninsured people covers only 10 states for five years, and excludes uninsured individuals who qualify for Marketplace premium tax credits.

The bill contains no offset funding for insurers' added coverage costs; the original bill's own sense of Congress said later legislation should provide an offset for federal costs, and an honest supporter would concede the mandate may nudge premiums up for everyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insured insulin users this is a straightforward, well-targeted benefit: a hard $35 monthly cap, no deductible, no prior authorization, for a drug people cannot skip. The design is imperfect — it caps patient cost-sharing rather than list prices, leaves insurers free to pick which products get the cap, and excludes out-of-network fills, so its real-world savings depend on how plans and manufacturers respond. The committee version is materially weaker than what was introduced: the cap starts a year later and the PBM rebate pass-through — the part that would have exposed and returned the middleman take — is gone. Even the weakened version would still put a hard ceiling on what insulin users pay out of pocket, and the competition provisions attack the delays that have kept cheaper biosimilars off the market.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved the bill in July and reported it to the Senate calendar in August 2026, where it sits waiting for a floor vote no one has scheduled yet.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) introduced the INSULIN Act of 2026 on March 25, 2026, joined by 28 original cosponsors from both parties.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
On July 22, 2026, the HELP Committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On August 7, 2026, Sen. Cassidy reported the bill with a complete substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 552.
The committee substitute delays the $35 cost-sharing cap from plan years beginning in 2027 to plan years beginning in 2028.

The committee substitute removed the original bill's Title II, which had required pharmacy benefit managers, third-party administrators, and insurers to remit 100% of insulin rebates, fees, and other remuneration to the health plan with full disclosure and audit rights.

The committee substitute also loosened the citizen-petition timeliness requirement from 60 days after a petitioner knew the relevant information to 180 days, and added a condition that biosimilar expedited review applies only after all exclusivity periods expired at least three years prior.
No floor vote has taken place and the 119th Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand insulin makers and pharmacy benefit managers are better off than they would have been under the bill as introduced: the version cleared by the committee delayed the patient cap by a year, deleted the requirement that middlemen return 100% of insulin rebates to health plans, and eased the deadline for petitions that can delay biosimilar approvals. Insulin users gained a bipartisan committee endorsement but are still waiting for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The 28 cosponsors split 14 Republicans, 13 Democrats, and 1 Independent, and a Republican senator reported the bill to the calendar; no opponent appears anywhere in the action record.

industries.note: The bill curtails the tools — delay petitions and slow biosimilar review — that have kept cheaper copies of insulin off the market, and the $35 patient cap pressures the high-net-price model. Even after the committee weakened the bill, the competition provisions remain a direct threat to insulin monopoly pricing.

PBMs and third-party administrators take a share of insulin rebates and fees; the original bill would have required them to remit 100% of that money back to health plans with disclosure and audit rights. The committee rewrite deleted that section — a substantial reprieve for the middleman business model.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans must cover selected insulin at a $35 monthly cap with no deductible or prior authorization, and absorb that cost without federal offset funding, likely nudging premiums. But the 'selected products' structure lets them steer patients toward whichever insulin maximizes their rebates, and the rewrite delayed the cap to 2028.
Expedited FDA review, faster facility reinspections, and curbs on delay petitions clear the path for cheaper biosimilar insulin competitors to reach the market.

industries.industry: Community health centers and retail pharmacies
industries.note: The 10-state pilot program funds FQHC on-site pharmacies and retail community pharmacies to dispense insulin at $35 or less to uninsured patients.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee and sits on the Senate calendar under General Orders — meaning it is eligible for a floor vote, but only if Senate leaders schedule one. Many bipartisan health bills reach this point and stall at the end of a two-year Congress. Its broad 14-13-1 bipartisan sponsorship and a friendly committee report give it a real path, but it would still need a Senate floor vote and then passage in the House before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
